new_statements.quote: 4.17.1. Syllable structure: CV and V (Elugbe 1973). [...] 4.17.8. Tone: Ibilo exhibits a 'two tone plus downstep' system. There is no evidence of synchronic downdrifting in my data, although Akinlabi (1979) rather routinely claimed downdrift exists in Ibilo. One notices that Akinlabi presents no instrumental evidence of downdrift even though he presents such evidence to show that high, low, etc., tones occur. The downstep in Ibilo is limited in occurrence and is unlikely to be successfully analysed as a 'mid' tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ibilo is described as a level-tone language (High vs Low, plus a restricted non-automatic downstep); neither this sketch nor Elugbe's 1973 thesis sketch (pp.241-265: "Two levels of pitch are significant in Ibilo: high and low") says anything about word stress or accent, and the word 'stress' does not occur in the 1989 book.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal details: downstep occurs only in a few grammatical contexts (e.g. past progressive); LL disyllabic nouns surface as high-falling-low in isolation (Elugbe 1973: 263-265); final vowels of disyllabic stems are devoiced/shortened (Elugbe 1989: 42, after Akinlabi 1979).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical/word-level tone on CV and V syllables; data are citation forms and short phrases from one or two Ibillo-town speakers (J.T.D. Orisanaiye, Joel Elegbe). Elugbe himself warns (1989: 47) that his examination of tone in most languages 'could not have been anything but superficial'.
new_statements.identity_note: 'Ibilo' [ibil1238] is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid: ISO 639-3 [ibi] was retired in 2012 (CR 2011-153) and merged into Okpamheri [opa], okpa1238 (Edoid > North-Western Edoid > Southern NWE). Elugbe's 1973 and 1989 sketches explicitly describe 'the Ibilo dialect of Okpamheri', i.e. Okpamheri as spoken in Ibillo town (Akoko-Edo LGA, Edo State), data from J.T.D. Orisanaiye and Joel Elegbe. Note Glottolog's okpa1238 dialect list (Emhalhe, Okulosho, Western Okpamheri sub-groups) has no separate 'Ibilo' node; Elugbe 1989 treats Emhalhe (Somorika) as a distinct Okpamheri dialect with a more complex (3-level) tone system, so the statement quoted here should be attached to Ibilo/Ibillo specifically, and by extension to okpa1238 only with that caveat.

sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent (the word 'stress' does not occur in the book). Ibilo sketch: syllable structure CV and V; 4.17.8 Tone p.95: "Ibilo exhibits a 'two tone plus downstep' system"; downstep limited, not analysable as a mid tone. Also p.42: final-vowel devoicing/shortening in Ibilo disyllabic stems (Akinlabi 1979).

sources.note: No stress/accent statement. Sec.6 Tone pp.263-264: "Two levels of pitch are significant in Ibilo: high and low" with minimal triplet; a third (downstep) level not found in lexical items; sec.7 pp.264-265 disyllabic noun tone classes LL/LH/HL/HH, LL nouns surface high-falling-low. General p.90: Ibilo grouped under 'two tones plus downstep'.
